column4: Adam is promised that he will not suffer the sun's exposed heat, וَلَا تَضْحَىٰ; this supplies the section's exact meeting of ḍuḥā exposure with the story of losing and receiving guidance.
After Adam's fall, his Lord chooses him, turns to him, and guides him; this is the section's sequence of a dependent person being reclaimed and led.
The descent is followed by promised guidance, and whoever follows it فَلَا يَضِلُّ وَلَا يَشْقَىٰ; loss of way and relief from misery meet exactly as the section describes.

The Prophet did not know the Book or faith, then revelation became a light by which God guides, and he guides to a straight path; this joins the section's prophetic addressee, light, and guidance without implying culpable error.
God's completing His favor to the Prophet and guiding him on a straight path, وَيُتِمَّ نِعْمَتَهُ ... وَيَهْدِيَكَ, directly joins completed gift to guidance.
Fear of poverty, عَيْلَةً, is answered by a future promise, فَسَوْفَ يُغْنِيكُمُ ٱللَّهُ مِن فَضْلِهِۦ; this is the section's exact meeting of delay and sufficiency.
Being content with what God and His messenger give is coupled to confidence that God will give again from His bounty; the verse gathers gift, رضوا, future provision, and sufficiency in one response.
وَهُوَ ٱلْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِۦ locates irresistible qahr above all servants, clarifying why a servant may not enact downward qahr upon an orphan.
The only other Qur'anic prohibition with تَنْهَرْ pairs “do not rebuke them” with “say to them a noble word”; it states the gentle voice that replaces the section's forbidden voice.
The prayer كَمَا رَبَّيَانِى صَغِيرًا makes having been raised the reason for merciful humility, just as the section turns remembered nurture into a duty toward the vulnerable.

Mary's Lord causes her to grow well, places her in Zakariyya's care, and he repeatedly finds provision with her; رب, guardianship, finding, growth, and provision converge in one dependent child's scene.
Moses sees a fire from afar and hopes either for a brand or أَجِدُ عَلَى ٱلنَّارِ هُدًى; a visible light becomes the hoped-for place of finding guidance.
قَدْ أُوتِيتَ سُؤْلَكَ يَـٰمُوسَىٰ answers Moses's request before recounting earlier favors, matching the section's movement from a granted desire to remembered gift.
God explicitly narrates an earlier favor to Moses, وَلَقَدْ مَنَنَّا عَلَيْكَ مَرَّةً أُخْرَىٰ, enacting the section's command to bring a Lord-given favor into speech.
The earlier favor begins with revelation to Moses's mother; this row supplies the divine initiative whose concrete instructions continue in 20:39.
The infant is cast into the chest and river, taken by an enemy, covered with divine love, and reared under God's eye; exposure, apparent loss, ownership, and nurture meet here.

Moses's sister leads to a carer, he is returned so his mother's eye may be comforted, rescued after killing a man, tried, and brought from Midian “according to a measure”; it compresses the section's shelter-road-provision life sequence.
وَٱصْطَنَعْتُكَ لِنَفْسِى completes the infant's being fashioned under God's eye by naming the Lord's deliberate forming and choosing of him.
Moses's mother is told to nurse him, cast him into the river when afraid, and trust the promise of return; loss, provision, protection, and future restoration occupy one command.
Pharaoh's household picks up the exposed infant, placing the found child inside the very house that will oppose him; it supplies the dangerous human “finder” in the continuing rescue scene.
Pharaoh's wife calls the found infant a comfort to the eye and proposes taking him as a son; the apparently ownerless child is offered a household and protection from killing.
Moses's mother's heart becomes empty and nearly discloses him until God binds her heart; the verse gives the inward cost of the loss whose outward search continues in 28:11.
The mother tells Moses's sister to follow him, and she watches from afar without being recognized; this is the searching side of the section's lost-and-finder pair.
After other nurses are withheld, the sister offers to show a household that will care sincerely for the child; guidance, household, and nurture become the means of finding his proper carer.
God returns Moses to his mother so her eye is comforted and she knows the promise is true; the lost infant is found, housed, and restored to رضا-like relief.
On setting out toward Midian, Moses says that perhaps his Lord will guide him to the level way; the traveler who does not know his route asks رب for direction.

At Midian's water Moses finds two women holding back their flock while the other herders water, and learns that their father is old; finding, herd, vulnerable dependents, and absent shepherd meet visibly.

Moses waters the women's flock, withdraws to shade, and confesses to his Lord that he is فقير for whatever good is sent; the helper stands at once on the giving and needy sides of the section's scene.
One woman returns modestly with a father's invitation to reward Moses for watering, and the father gives him safety; provision for an act of care becomes admission into a protective household.
The daughter recommends employing Moses as strong and trustworthy; this verse supplies the judgment that turns the unprovided traveler into a supported member of the household.
The father offers one of his daughters in marriage in exchange for a fixed term of service; the lost and poor traveler is given family, home, and measured livelihood.
Moses accepts either measured term without injustice and makes God trustee over the agreement; it makes consent, limit, and divine oversight explicit in the new household.
After completing the term, Moses travels with his family and sees a fire, hoping for news or a brand; completed provision leads back to the light-at-a-distance road scene.
Pharaoh's أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا uses the nurture branch of رب while claiming ownership of the child raised in his house.
Moses describes his former state as وَأَنَا۠ مِنَ ٱلضَّآلِّينَ; in context it is the unknowing state from which flight, judgment, and mission follow.
A caravan's water-drawer brings up Joseph and announces a boy, then the finders conceal him as merchandise; a lost child is “found” while his true belonging is ignored.
The Egyptian buyer tells his wife to honor Joseph's lodging and perhaps adopt him, while God establishes him and teaches him; the found child receives a house and gradual formation.
Joseph refuses the coercive invitation by saying his rabb/master has made his lodging good; the human-master sense of رب appears inside the lost child's shelter story.
Jacob sends his sons to search attentively for Joseph and his brother and forbids despair of God's relief; it supplies the searching owner-parent side of a long-lost person's recovery.
Joseph, once the lost child given lodging, takes his parents into his own shelter, آوَىٰٓ إِلَيْهِ أَبَوَيْهِ; the sheltered one has become the shelterer.
Joseph recounts his Lord's past kindness in release and family reunion after drawing his parents near; a completed life sequence is turned into spoken divine favor.
Moses declares that he will keep traveling until he reaches the meeting of the two seas; purposeful seeking opens a journey whose lost sign will lead him to a guide.
At the meeting place Moses and his servant lose track of their fish as it takes its path into the sea; losing the object marks the place they were seeking.
The servant remembers the forgotten fish and its astonishing path at the rock; the forgotten loss becomes articulated guidance back to the meeting place.
Moses says “that is what we were seeking” and they retrace their footprints; search, recovery, and a road reversed join in one action.
They find a servant given mercy and taught knowledge by God; the journey's lost sign ends in finding the human guide.
Moses asks to follow the found servant so that he may be taught some of the guidance given him; the former guide takes the position of a traveler asking for guidance.
God guides seekers of His pleasure to paths of peace, brings them from darkness into light, and guides to a straight path; light and road are explicitly one guidance movement.
A person made alive after death is given a light by which to walk among people, opposite one trapped in darkness; new life, visibility, and traversable way meet exactly.
Revelation brings people from darkness into light by their Lord's permission and onto His path; the Lord makes both sight and road possible.
Night and day are two signs: the night sign is effaced and the day sign made visible so people may seek bounty and reckon years; covering, visible road, provision, and time meet in one ayah.
God makes night a covering, sleep a rest, and day a rising; the section's cover-light movement deepens into a daily image of death and renewed emergence.
A perpetual night is posed as a world in which no other god can bring light; the question makes visible light a divine provision, continued by the night-day purposes in 28:73.
A perpetual day is posed against the night in which people rest; it gives the necessary limit to exposure before 28:73 reunites rest and provision.
Night for rest and day for seeking God's bounty are named together as mercy; covering and light become complementary forms of provision.
The oath by the day إِذَا جَلَّىٰهَا makes daylight the act of disclosure, matching the section's movement from covered night to manifest gift.
The following oath by the night إِذَا يَغْشَىٰهَا makes night a covering, the direct counterpart to 91:3's disclosure.
وَٱلَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَىٰ repeats the section's night-as-cover action in another oath that will lead to giving and self-sufficiency.
وَٱلنَّهَارِ إِذَا تَجَلَّىٰ answers the covering night with a day that becomes manifest, preparing the same surah's contrast between giver and self-sufficient miser.
A kind word and forgiveness are declared better than charity followed by hurt; this directly joins the giving hand to the gentle voice that must accompany it.
Guardians must hand orphans their property and not consume it by substitution; it states the section's concrete prohibition on a stronger hand taking from an orphan.
Those managing property must provide food and clothing from it and speak a fitting word; material care and gentle speech are one guardianship duty.
Orphans are tested until maturity, then their property is handed over with witnesses, while rich guardians abstain and poor ones take only fairly; nurture, consent, and limits replace qahr.
When orphans and the needy attend a distribution, they are to receive something and be addressed with a fitting word; hand and voice jointly protect the excluded.
The ban on consuming one another's wealth makes mutually willing trade, عَن تَرَاضٍ, the lawful alternative; it supplies the consent that the section sets opposite forced taking.
The relative, needy person, and traveler are each to be given their due; the command turns received provision outward toward dependent and road-bound people.
If one must turn away while awaiting future mercy from one's Lord, one must still speak a gentle word; deferred provision is joined directly to non-rebuking speech.
The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor wholly outstretched; this gives a bodily measure to the giving hand in the surrounding needy-person passage.
The Lord expands and measures provision with full knowledge of His servants; it names the divine provision behind both present inability and hoped-for future giving in 17:28.
A wall preserves treasure for two orphan boys until they reach maturity, because their father was righteous and their Lord willed mercy; unseen guardianship protects the orphan's future property.
David and Solomon judge a field into which a people's sheep strayed by night; night, an uncontrolled herd, ownership, and responsibility meet in one legal scene.
God makes Solomon understand the judgment and gives both prophets wisdom; divine guidance resolves the night-herd dispute introduced in 21:78.
The Prophet's frown and turning away stage the rebuff that the section's command forbids; 80:2 identifies the vulnerable person who approached.
The reason for the rebuff is that the blind man came to him; this verse supplies the dependent seeker in the corrected encounter.
The addressee is reminded that the seeker may purify himself; it reveals what a harsh reception could withhold from the one who came.
The seeker may remember and benefit from the reminder; the proper answer to his approach is useful speech, not dismissal.
The one who comes striving is set opposite the person treated as self-sufficient; his active approach sharpens the section's responsibility toward a sāʾil.
The approaching person also fears God; this makes his outward dependence carry inward moral seriousness.
The rebuke is that the addressee is distracted from the striving, fearful seeker; it is a direct prophetic correction of turning away.
A person interprets expanded provision as “my Lord has honored me”; the verse opens the false equation between wealth and divine regard that 89:16-18 overturn.
When provision is measured tightly, the same person says “my Lord has humiliated me”; this exposes the felt humiliation of poverty before the orphan commands correct the diagnosis.
The response “No” is followed by the charge that they do not honor the orphan; true reception of divine provision is measured by treatment of the dependent.
They do not urge one another to feed the poor; the verse converts the mistaken wealth judgment into the same duty toward need found in the section.
The person has not attempted the steep path; the road image becomes a moral passage whose concrete acts toward captives, orphans, and the poor follow.
“What will make you know what the steep path is?” announces that the following care acts define the path rather than merely ornament it.
Freeing a neck is the first act that crosses the steep path, reversing domination by releasing the person under another's power.
Feeding on a day of hunger makes provision in scarcity part of walking the steep path.
The recipient is an orphan of near kin; path and orphan-care meet explicitly.
The alternative recipient is a poor person in the dust; the path culminates in raising the lowly rather than passing over him.
The giving sequence begins with the one who gives and is mindful; this is the active answer expected from someone who has received sufficiency.
The giver confirms the best promise, supplying the trust in future good that makes giving possible.
God promises to ease the giver toward ease; future divine facilitation answers the person's present act of giving.
The protected person gives his wealth to purify himself; the hand enriched by God becomes a giving hand.
He is not repaying a favor owed to another person; this prevents the gift from becoming a coercive human claim of ownership.
He gives only seeking the face of his Lord Most High; رب and the “above” position are redirected from human domination to divine رضا.
The giver will soon be satisfied, وَلَسَوْفَ يَرْضَىٰ; the phrase closes the giver's sequence with the same deferred رضا promised in the section.
The denier is identified as the one who violently repels the orphan; this is the clearest enacted opposite of “do not overpower the orphan.”
He does not urge feeding the poor; the failure toward need continues from physical repulsion into withheld provision.
Moses and Aaron are commanded to speak gently even to Pharaoh; soft speech is required in the very encounter with the human imitator of qahr.
The Prophet's divinely given gentleness keeps people near, whereas harshness and hardness of heart would scatter them; soft voice and receptive heart are causally joined.
The human is told to remember that God created him before when he was nothing; it states the section's “what was not becomes” layer of new creation.
Humans are created from earth, returned to it, and brought out from it once more; burial becomes the middle movement between two creations.
God causes humanity to grow from the earth like a growth; the nurturing image is extended into bodily creation from soil.
He then returns people to the earth and brings them out again; the covered dead becomes a renewed emergence.
A span of time passed when the human was not a thing mentioned; nonexistence, time, and eventual mention meet the section's “becoming” and speaking images.
God causes the human to die and assigns him a grave; it supplies the section's covered and earth-given corpse.
Then, whenever He wills, God raises that human; the grave of 80:21 opens onto new creation rather than abandonment.
Those who ask to be deferred to a near term are answered that worldly enjoyment is little and the Hereafter better; it is the section's exact postponement-and-better-end meeting.
People prefer the nearer worldly life; this names the preference corrected by the section's “the later is better.”
وَٱلْءَاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ states both the greater worth and greater endurance of the later life.
Each person spends according to means, including one whose provision is measured tightly, and God promises ease after hardship; provision received sets the measure of provision given.
The unmarried are to be married, and if they are poor God will enrich them from His bounty; marriage and household become the promised route from poverty to sufficiency, as in Moses's Midian scene.
Those unable to marry remain chaste until God enriches them from His bounty; delayed household and delayed sufficiency are held together.
Disclosing charity is good, while concealing it for the poor is better; it marks the boundary between openly recounting God's favor and protecting a recipient through hidden giving.
A powerless owned servant is contrasted with one granted good provision who spends from it secretly and openly; received sufficiency is made visible through free giving.
The Prophet is commanded to glorify his Lord before sunrise, before sunset, and through parts of night so that he may be satisfied; light-times, speech, رب, and رضا meet.
The human is charged to thank God and parents after recalling the mother's weakness and two years of nurture; remembered raising is converted into grateful conduct.
After recalling pregnancy, birth, and growth to maturity, the adult asks to thank God for favors to him and his parents and to act rightly; nurture culminates in spoken gratitude and outward duty.
The repeated وَهُوَ ٱلْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِۦ accompanies divine guardians and the taking of souls, reserving ultimate “above” qahr to the Lord rather than a human over the weak.
Pharaoh's chiefs propose killing sons and sparing women, and he boasts وَإِنَّا فَوْقَهُمْ قَـٰهِرُونَ; human qahr “above them” is staged as murderous imitation of divine sovereignty.
Pharaoh exalts himself, divides the people, and slaughters sons while sparing women; the ruler turns power over dependent children into corruption rather than shelter.
Pharaoh calls Moses's former deed ingratitude immediately after claiming to have raised him; human nurture is weaponized as a debt and accusation.
Moses answers that he fled in fear, then his Lord gave him judgment and made him a messenger; the coercive household's claim is displaced by the true Lord's rescue and gift.
Moses rejects Pharaoh's claimed “favor” because Pharaoh enslaved the Children of Israel; it is the boundary between narrating divine favor and using a supposed gift to erase oppression.
The owner of ninety-nine ewes demands the other man's single ewe and overpowers him in speech; flock, taking without رضا, and coercive voice meet in one counter-scene.
David identifies the demand for the single ewe as injustice and generalizes that partners often transgress; judgment sets a limit on the stronger owner's grasp.
The person who considers himself self-sufficient, ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ, receives attention; this is the wrongly favored pole opposite the dependent seeker.
The Prophet is reproved for attending to the self-sufficient person; it reverses the section's priority toward the one who comes in need.
The addressee is not responsible if that self-sufficient person does not purify himself; the verse removes the rationale for neglecting the vulnerable seeker.
They consume inheritance with devouring greed after failing the orphan and poor; the taking hand is shown at its harshest.
Their excessive love of wealth names the heart-state behind withholding and devouring, opposite رضا with what the Lord gives.
The counterfigure withholds and deems himself self-sufficient, بَخِلَ وَٱسْتَغْنَىٰ; enrichment becomes a false independence that blocks giving.
He denies the best promise, reversing the giver's trust in future good.
God eases the withholding, self-sufficient person toward hardship; it reverses the future ease promised to the giver.
The human transgresses; 96:7 identifies perceived self-sufficiency as the trigger, warning what may happen after enrichment.
أَن رَّءَاهُ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ makes seeing oneself self-sufficient the cause of overstepping, the exact moral danger when the formerly poor person stands above another.
People love the immediate life, ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ, making haste rather than deferred good their governing desire.
They leave the Hereafter, the direct reversal of the section's claim that the later is better.
Charity is invalidated by reminders of generosity and hurt; this limits public speech about favor so that the giver does not turn gift into domination of its recipient.
In the other Adam descent account, guidance is promised after the fall, and its followers need not fear or grieve; it confirms the same fall-then-guidance structure as 20:123.
Righteousness includes giving loved wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, travelers, and askers; several recipients of the section's final commands are gathered under one giving act.
Those who spend and do not follow their gifts with reminders or injury receive security from their Lord; the verse protects the receiver from the giver's later verbal qahr.
Restrained poor people may be mistaken for self-sufficient because they do not beg insistently; it makes hidden need the test of a giver who sees beyond the audible request.
A debtor in hardship must be given time until ease, while remitting the debt is better; delay becomes mercy directed toward another person's insufficiency.
The answer about spending names parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers; received good is routed toward both those who raised a person and those now dependent on him.
Orphan property may be approached only in the best way until maturity; it draws a firm boundary around the guardian's stronger hand.
The same orphan-property limit is joined to fulfilling covenants; guardianship is accountable stewardship rather than ownership.
The wealthy acknowledge in their property a right for both the asker and the deprived; the asking voice calls forth a due rather than a rebuke.
Those who pray assign a recognized share in their wealth; 70:25 names the asker and deprived as its owners.
The assigned share belongs to the asker and the deprived; this turns response to need from discretionary favor into acknowledged right.
They feed the poor, orphan, and captive despite loving or needing the food; provision is passed onward without waiting for abundance.
They say they seek neither repayment nor thanks from recipients; the giving hand renounces the coercive claim that a favor creates.
The Helpers give preference to others despite their own need and feel no inward want over what others receive; scarcity, رضا, and outward generosity are reconciled.
وَأَنَّهُۥ هُوَ أَغْنَىٰ وَأَقْنَىٰ identifies God as the one who enriches and grants sufficiency, reinforcing the true source behind the section's passive receipt.
All people are the poor before God while God alone is the self-sufficient, praiseworthy one; it keeps human enrichment from becoming imagined independence.
People are invited to spend, yet some withhold; God is the rich one and they are the poor, reversing any claim that the giver owns sufficiency in himself.
God measures and then guides, وَٱلَّذِى قَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ; fitted measure and direction are two aspects of the Lord's ordering.
God promises the prophetic addressee facilitation toward ease; it parallels the section's future promise without repeating its gift language.
Ease is asserted with hardship to the same prophetic addressee after remembered favors; relief is present within constriction rather than merely after it.
The repeated promise of ease stabilizes the future-facing reassurance before the following commands to act and turn to the Lord.
God as guardian brings believers from darkness into light, while false patrons reverse the movement; ownership and illumination are joined through the identity of the true guardian.
Layered darkness leaves a person scarcely able to see his own hand, and one denied God's light has no light; it gives the section's hand image a concrete boundary of invisibility.
Night is made a garment, a compact image of the covering that the section hears in night.
Day is made a time of livelihood, joining visible day to the provision for which people go out.
God makes night for rest and day giving sight; darkness and visibility are complementary provisions rather than abandonment and return.
Night is made for rest and day as something visible, and the arrangement is called divine bounty; light-dark alternation itself is narrated as favor.
People were dead, are given life, will die, and will be brought back; the verse states the full transformation behind the section's grave-and-new-creation layer.
God brings living from dead and dead from living and revives earth after death; emergence from burial is placed within a recurring reversal.
Human formation from dust through measured womb stages and the revival of barren earth are offered as evidence of resurrection; growth, nurture, earth, and new creation form one argument.
Gratitude for divine favor is promised increase, while ingratitude has consequence; it gives ethical force to speaking and acknowledging the Lord's gift.
When all are brought forth with nothing hidden, the question of dominion is answered: it belongs to God, the One, the Overpowering; exposure after death and ultimate qahr coincide.
The argument against rival lords culminates in God as the One, the Overpowering; it ties the owner sense of rabb to the unique bearer of absolute qahr.
